slides.title: Best-First Search, A*, and Heuristic Quality

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: Lesson six adds informed judgment to the frontier. OPEN still stores generated candidates, CLOSED still records expanded states, g of n still measures cost already paid, and parent links still recover a route. The new ingredient is h of n: a problem-specific estimate of the cost that remains. Read the three visible cards as a progression: h alone for greedy selection, g plus h for.

segments.label: Worked mechanism
segments.text: Think of planning a road trip. Greedy best-first stares at the remaining map distance, while A-star also checks the fuel already burned. One behaves like an impatient tourist pointing at the destination; the other keeps both the receipt and the compass on the dashboard. If two frontier states have h values two and five but their g values are one hundred and one, greedy prefers.

segments.label: Boundary and guarantee
segments.text: A heuristic is guidance, not prophecy. A small h value can make a state look attractive without proving that the full route through it is cheap. The central question is therefore not merely which number is smallest, but what that number means and what guarantee it supports. OPEN and CLOSED organize the computation; neither list magically creates optimality. Optimality comes from the evaluation rule, the.

segments.text: By the end, you should be able to trace greedy best-first and A-star, prove admissibility or consistency, compare heuristic strength, and reject A-star when the environment is dynamic, uncertain, or adversarial. The algorithm name comes after the model and assumptions, never before them. Keep four columns in your notes: selected state, g, h, and f. slides.title: Follow the smallest estimated distance to the goal

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: Greedy best-first search removes from OPEN whichever node has minimum h of n. The heuristic estimates remaining goal cost, so the rule says, choose what currently looks closest. It ignores the path cost already accumulated, which makes the method energetic, focused, and occasionally spectacularly gullible. segments.label: Worked mechanism
segments.text: Imagine hiking toward a mountain by always walking toward the peak as the crow flies. A cliff can make the visually closest position a terrible route. Greedy search behaves similarly: it may race down a promising-looking branch while a slightly less glamorous frontier node begins a much cheaper path. With frontier entries X having h equals two and Y having h equals four, greedy selects.

segments.label: Boundary and guarantee
segments.text: OPEN is a minimum-priority queue keyed here by h. CLOSED is an explored record used for duplicate handling. Parent pointers recover the selected route, and a best-g record can detect an improved duplicate even though g does not decide which greedy node leaves OPEN next. A heap usually supports logarithmic insertion and removal, while a state-indexed map supports fast duplicate lookup. Calling CLOSED a queue.

segments.label: Transfer and takeaway
segments.text: Greedy best-first is not generally optimal, and in unrestricted spaces it is not generally complete. A neat priority queue does not repair those limits. It merely executes the chosen policy efficiently, like a very organized assistant following an overconfident instruction. Before using greedy search, ask whether a locally low estimate correlates with progress, whether cycles are controlled, and whether any solution is sufficient. If minimum-cost.

slides.title: Generate broadly, then select the most promising frontier node

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: The procedure begins by placing the start node in OPEN and leaving CLOSED empty. It repeatedly removes a minimum-h node, performs the goal test, generates legal successors, handles duplicates, records parent information, and continues until a goal is selected or OPEN becomes empty. Walk down the numbered list in order. Removing, goal-testing, expanding, inserting, updating, and closing are distinct events; changing their order can change.

segments.label: Worked mechanism
segments.text: The crucial distinction from hill climbing is memory of alternatives. Greedy best-first may follow one branch deeply, but siblings remain in OPEN. When the favorite branch disappoints, the algorithm chooses the next-best waiting entry instead of declaring that the universe has personally betrayed it. slides.title: An admissible heuristic never overestimates remaining optimal cost

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: Admissibility is a pointwise property of h. Let h-star of n be the true optimal remaining cost from n to a goal. An admissible heuristic satisfies zero less than or equal to h of n, less than or equal to h-star of n, for every relevant state. Misplaced tiles is admissible for the unit-cost eight-puzzle because every misplaced tile must be addressed by future motion..

segments.label: Worked mechanism
segments.text: Enlarge the definition and interpret h as a lower-bound price tag. If the cheapest remaining trip truly costs twelve, estimates zero, seven, or twelve are admissible; thirteen is not. The estimate may be pessimistically small, but it may never promise a cost larger than reality. Admissible does not mean accurate. The zero heuristic is perfectly admissible and perfectly unhelpful about direction. It preserves A-star's safety.

action.label: Enlarge the source figure while explaining it

segments.label: Boundary and guarantee
segments.text: Admissibility belongs to the heuristic, not automatically to greedy selection. Tree-search A-star can use an admissible h to obtain optimality under standard nonnegative-cost and termination conditions. Graph-search A-star also needs consistency or a correct reopening policy. Negative estimates are usually excluded because they cease to represent remaining cost and can distort ordering. Nonnegative edge costs and suitable termination assumptions also matter; the inequality alone does.

segments.label: Transfer and takeaway
segments.text: At a goal, h should be zero because no remaining cost is required. To prove a heuristic admissible, identify the relaxed problem or lower-bound argument that prevents overestimation; familiarity, popularity, or a confident textbook font is not a proof. Close the figure and test one proposed h value against h-star. One counterexample is sufficient to disprove admissibility, while a proof must cover every state in.

slides.title: Three questions expose three common confusions

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: Question one asks whether admissible means perfect. No. The defining inequality permits underestimation; exact equality with h-star would be a perfect heuristic, usually as expensive as already knowing the solution. Admissibility is a safety ceiling, not a demand for clairvoyance. Use the first tab to separate admissible from perfect, then move the focus to the answer-and-proof sequence. A lower estimate can waste work without violating.

segments.label: Worked mechanism
segments.text: Question two asks about eight-puzzle heuristics. Misplaced tiles and Manhattan distance are admissible with standard unit-cost moves. Each needs a lower-bound argument. Any mysterious third heuristic must be checked pointwise rather than admitted to the club because its name sounds mathematical. On the second tab, explain why one legal move changes tile distances in a controlled way. The proof is tied to the move model.

segments.label: Boundary and guarantee
segments.text: Question three exposes abbreviation trouble. BFS might mean breadth-first search or best-first search. Breadth-first equals uniform-cost, and therefore A-star with h zero, only under equal positive step costs. Greedy best-first orders by h alone and is not A-star. On the third tab, say breadth-first and greedy best-first in full. This is not vocabulary fussiness: the two algorithms prioritize different quantities and support different guarantees.

segments.label: Transfer and takeaway
segments.text: The proof habit is the takeaway. For a heuristic claim, write the relevant inequality and the cost assumptions. For an algorithm claim, state the search variant, graph policy, branching, edge costs, and termination conditions. Acronyms cannot carry those assumptions for you. For each response, ask what evidence would falsify it. A single overestimating state defeats admissibility, an edge violation defeats consistency, and unequal step costs.

Choosing by only h ignores sunk travel, while choosing by only g ignores direction. A-star balances both ledgers. For frontier X with g four and h nine, f is thirteen. An admissible h makes f a lower bound on the cost of any solution through n. That lower-bound interpretation is what supports A-star's comparison.

segments.label: Transfer and takeaway
segments.text: Two special cases clarify the rule. If h is zero everywhere, A-star becomes uniform-cost search. If g is omitted, the behavior becomes greedy best-first. The missing term reveals which information and which guarantees have been discarded. Keep units compatible: if g is minutes and h is kilometers, addition produces numerical soup. slides.title: Equal depth is not the same as equal estimated total cost

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: Breadth-first search orders by depth, while A-star orders by estimated total cost. Those rankings coincide only under special conditions. Equal depth says the same number of actions; it does not say those actions have equal cost or lead equally close to the goal. A two-edge route costing one hundred per edge is shallower than a three-edge route costing one per edge. Breadth-first prefers the former.

segments.label: Worked mechanism

slides.title: Set h(n)=0 and A* becomes uniform-cost search

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: Setting h of n to zero simplifies f equals g plus zero, so A-star orders the frontier entirely by accumulated path cost. On nonnegative weighted graphs, this is uniform-cost or Dijkstra-style search: settle the least-cost reachable frontier record next. The zero heuristic is admissible and consistent, but it provides no directional information. It is the safe baseline against which stronger heuristics should demonstrate search savings.

segments.text: Enlarge the definition and picture a triangle. Going directly from the estimate at n cannot claim more remaining distance than taking one real step and then using the successor's estimate. A violation is a heuristic price tag that falls suspiciously faster than the journey pays for. Manhattan distance is consistent for standard unit-cost puzzle moves because one legal tile move changes the total Manhattan estimate.

kinetics.label: Consistency violation

action.label: Enlarge the source figure while explaining it

segments.label: Boundary and guarantee
segments.text: Consistency makes f values nondecreasing along a path. Substitute g of n-prime equals g of n plus the edge cost, add terms, and the edge inequality yields f of n-prime greater than or equal to f of n. Consistency is stronger than admissibility in the usual setting. An admissible heuristic may still have local drops that force graph-search A-star to reconsider CLOSED states.

segments.label: Transfer and takeaway
segments.text: Under standard graph-search conditions, consistency implies admissibility and allows A-star to close a state at its best g without later reopening it. If one edge violates the inequality, a cheaper route may reach an already expanded state. Close the figure and perform the diagnostic in a fixed order: write h at the source, edge cost, h at the successor, compute the right side, then compare.

slides.title: An inconsistent heuristic can force a CLOSED node to reopen

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: This graph uses an admissible but inconsistent heuristic. Start at S with g zero and f three. Expanding S generates A with g three, f three, and B with g one, f four, so A is selected first and placed in CLOSED. Read OPEN and CLOSED after every click. The dramatic moment is not discovering G at cost five; it is discovering that a CLOSED.

segments.label: Worked mechanism
segments.text: Expanding A creates goal G with cost five. B is then selected, and edge B to A discovers a cheaper g for A: two instead of three. Consistency fails on that edge because h of B is three while one plus h of A is only one. All heuristic values remain at or below true remaining optimal cost, so admissibility is not the failed property..

segments.label: Boundary and guarantee
segments.text: The improved A must leave CLOSED and reopen with g two, f two. Re-expanding it updates the goal from cost five to cost four. Without reopening, the algorithm can preserve the early expensive parent and return the wrong cost. Reopening is not duplicate chaos. It is a disciplined response to a strictly improved path record: update g, update the parent, restore frontier eligibility, and propagate.

segments.label: Transfer and takeaway
segments.text: Finally G with g four is selected, returning path S to B to A to G. The lesson is implementation-specific: admissibility protects the lower bound, but graph search needs consistency or correct reopen logic to propagate improved paths. Use the final state to compare two hypothetical implementations. Permanent CLOSED returns five; reopen-aware graph search returns four. That one policy decision changes correctness.

segments.label: Reopen trace state 2
segments.text: Expand S. A enters OPEN with g three and f three; B enters with g one and f four. Minimum f selects A first even though B begins.

segments.label: Reopen trace state 3
segments.text: Expand A too early. It reaches G with total cost five and moves into CLOSED. That goal record is only a candidate because another frontier route may still.

segments.label: Reopen trace state 4
segments.text: Select B and discover B-to-A with new g two. This beats A's stored g three, so update A's parent, remove it from CLOSED, and restore frontier eligibility.

segments.label: Reopen trace state 5
segments.text: Re-expand improved A. Its edge to G now produces goal cost four rather than five. The reopened record propagates the cheaper prefix into the descendant path.

segments.label: Reopen trace state 6
segments.text: Select G at g four and finish with S-to-B-to-A-to-G. Compare this result with permanent CLOSED, which would have preserved the inferior cost-five route.

slides.title: A more informed admissible heuristic gives tighter lower bounds

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: For two admissible heuristics, h-two dominates h-one when h-one of n is less than or equal to h-two of n for every state. The larger values remain below h-star, so h-two supplies tighter lower bounds without sacrificing admissibility. Dominance is a for-every-state comparison, not a claim that one heuristic has a better average on a sample. One violating state defeats the pointwise relation.

segments.label: Worked mechanism
segments.text: Enlarge the definition and compare misplaced tiles with Manhattan distance in the standard eight-puzzle. Every misplaced tile contributes at least one unit of Manhattan distance, while some tiles are several squares away. Manhattan therefore dominates the simpler count pointwise. The zero heuristic is dominated by every nonnegative admissible heuristic. It provides the baseline lower bound and turns A-star into uniform-cost search.

action.label: Enlarge the source figure while explaining it

segments.label: Boundary and guarantee
segments.text: With comparable tie-breaking, A-star using the dominating heuristic typically expands no more nodes than A-star using the weaker one. Tighter lower bounds eliminate more frontier candidates whose estimated totals cannot beat the best solution cost. Tie-breaking can affect exactly which equal-f nodes expand, so empirical counts need controlled comparisons. The theoretical intuition remains that tighter safe bounds focus the frontier.

segments.label: Transfer and takeaway
segments.text: More informed does not mean free. Manhattan distance costs slightly more arithmetic than counting misplaced tiles, and sophisticated pattern databases require memory and preprocessing. Judge total problem-solving effort, not just the elegance of the estimate. Close the figure and evaluate a stronger proposed h. Prove it stays below h-star, then price its computation. A heuristic that saves ten expansions but costs a million operations per.

slides.title: Search savings must exceed the cost of control knowledge

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: The cost graph separates search effort from heuristic or control effort. As a heuristic becomes more informed, node expansion and rule application may fall, while preprocessing, memory, sensing, or per-node calculation rises. Their sum can form a U-shaped total-cost curve. The descending curve represents search or rule-application cost; the ascending curve represents acquiring and using control knowledge. The total is their vertical sum.

segments.label: Worked mechanism
segments.text: Enlarge the curves and locate the interior minimum. The left side spends little on guidance and pays for a huge search. The right side owns a magnificent heuristic department whose meetings cost more than the problem it was hired to solve. A pattern database may be expensive once but reused across thousands of puzzles, changing the amortized optimum. Workload frequency belongs in the analysis.

action.label: Enlarge the source figure while explaining it

segments.label: Boundary and guarantee
segments.text: Node count is therefore an incomplete metric. Record wall-clock time, memory, heuristic calls, preprocessing, and solution quality. A stronger heuristic can dominate mathematically yet lose end-to-end when its computation overwhelms saved expansions. A learned heuristic adds training data, inference latency, and possible guarantee violations. If optimality matters, the system may need calibration, bounding, or a safe fallback.

segments.label: Transfer and takeaway
segments.text: The engineering objective is minimum total effort subject to the required guarantee. Choose the heuristic granularity that pays for itself on the expected problem distribution, hardware, and reuse frequency rather than worshiping maximum informedness. Close the graph and propose an experiment: run identical instances with h zero, misplaced tiles, and Manhattan distance; measure both expansions and elapsed time, then explain any disagreement.

slides.title: Use one lens for h and another for the search algorithm

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: Before evaluating a claim, identify the object. A heuristic function is judged for admissibility, consistency, and informedness. A search algorithm is judged for completeness, optimality, time, and space under explicit conditions. Mixing the two lenses creates questions that sound technical but lack a defined test. Use the visible two-column framework like a diagnostic tool. First point to heuristic or algorithm, then select the corresponding inequality.

segments.label: Worked mechanism
segments.text: For h-one admissibility, check zero less than or equal to h-one of n less than or equal to h-star everywhere. For h-two consistency, check the triangle inequality on every edge. These are properties of estimates, not of DFS as a whole procedure. The first two tabs are valid heuristic questions. Each has a concrete mathematical test, so the answer can be proved or refuted with.

segments.label: Boundary and guarantee
segments.text: Asking whether DFS is consistent is a category mismatch under this definition. Evaluate DFS for completeness, optimality, time, and memory instead. Classical algorithm admissibility is an older synonym for guaranteed optimality, which is separate from heuristic admissibility. The DFS tab deliberately exposes the mismatch. Consistency could mean colloquial reliability, but in informed search it names a property of h; precise language prevents accidental theorem swapping.

segments.label: Transfer and takeaway
segments.text: Best-first completeness also needs the variant and assumptions. Greedy, A-star, and other best-first strategies use different priorities. State the space, cycles, branching, costs, and termination policy before placing a checkmark beside the algorithm. The remaining tabs show algorithm questions. Explain why the phrase best-first is too broad and why algorithm admissibility means returning an optimal solution rather than satisfying h less than or equal to.

segments.label: Property diagnosis 2
segments.text: Open the consistency prompt for h-two. Use the heuristic lens and check every edge inequality h of n no greater than cost plus successor h; one violating edge.

segments.label: Property diagnosis 3
segments.text: Open the DFS consistency prompt. This is the deliberate category mismatch: DFS has no heuristic h to test here, so evaluate completeness, optimality, time, and space under its.

segments.label: Property diagnosis 4
segments.text: Open the best-first completeness prompt. Name the exact variant before answering because greedy and A-star have different priorities, guarantees, and dependencies on cycles, branching, costs, and termination.

segments.label: Property diagnosis 5
segments.text: Open algorithm A admissibility. In classical algorithm language, admissible means guaranteed to return an optimal solution; it is not the pointwise lower-bound inequality used to judge a heuristic.

slides.title: Can all intelligent tasks use A*?

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: A-star is powerful when a task can be modeled as deterministic path search with states, actions, edge costs, a goal, and a defensible heuristic. The five cases test whether that model captures the central difficulty or merely one bounded component. For every case, use the same checklist before revealing the analysis: state, actions, edge cost, heuristic, observability, dynamics, and other agents. A-star is a conclusion.

segments.label: Worked mechanism
segments.text: For autopilot, A-star can plan a route through a known discretized region, but it is not the whole flight controller. Wind, partial observation, moving traffic, safety envelopes, and continuous dynamics require sensing, prediction, feedback, and online replanning around the path search. Autopilot may use graph search for a bounded route subproblem while control laws track the route and replanning reacts to change. Components can be.

segments.label: Boundary and guarantee
segments.text: For an autonomous drone and robot vacuum, A-star fits known-map point-to-point travel. Name configurations or grid cells as states, feasible moves as actions, and energy or distance as cost. Unknown rooms, moving obstacles, people, and pets demand additional online behavior. Drone and vacuum examples show discretization tradeoffs. Fine grids improve geometric fidelity but enlarge the search; coarse grids save computation but may erase safe passages.

segments.label: Transfer and takeaway
segments.text: Chess and financial investment reveal model failure. Chess is adversarial because another agent selects actions against us, so minimax-style reasoning is appropriate. Investment is stochastic, partially observed, dynamic, and risk-sensitive; a deterministic shortest path hides the problem we most need to solve. Chess has alternating agency, while investment has uncertain transitions and rewards. In both cases, the environment actively defeats the fixed deterministic graph assumption.

segments.label: Application 2 model
segments.text: Select the autonomous drone. Model grid cells or configurations as states, feasible motions as actions, and energy or distance as cost; then ask how wind and moving obstacles.

segments.label: Application 2 analysis
segments.text: Reveal the drone analysis. A-star is defensible for a discretized known planning map, while sensing and online replanning must handle uncertain motion, new obstacles, and changing local conditions.

segments.label: Application 3 model
segments.text: Select the robot vacuum. A floor-plan cell can be a state and travel distance an edge cost, but point-to-point routing is different from complete coverage and safe interaction.

segments.label: Application 3 analysis
segments.text: Reveal the vacuum analysis. A-star can route across a known map; mapping, coverage strategy, obstacle discovery, and reactive safety require additional algorithms around that route component.

segments.label: Application 4 model
segments.text: Select chess. Board positions and legal moves form a graph, yet an opponent deliberately chooses alternating actions. Ordinary shortest-path search does not represent that strategic control of successor.

segments.label: Application 4 analysis
segments.text: Reveal the chess analysis. Use adversarial search such as minimax and alpha-beta because the other player optimizes against us; A-star's passive deterministic environment assumption is the wrong model.

segments.label: Application 5 model
segments.text: Select financial investment. States, actions, and objectives can be written down, but returns are uncertain, observations incomplete, conditions dynamic, and risk essential. A single deterministic edge cost erases.

segments.label: Application 5 analysis
segments.text: Reveal the investment analysis. Decision-theoretic, stochastic, sequential, and risk-aware models are needed; A-star alone may optimize a simplified subproblem but cannot justify the overall investment policy.

slides.title: Offline deterministic search is only one corner of agency

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: Offline deterministic search assumes a known model, predictable actions, and enough stability to compute a path before execution. Real agents may act physically, observe partially, face stochastic outcomes, operate in changing worlds, or interact with cooperative and competitive agents. Move focus across the four limitation cards as each is named: physical action, uncertainty, change, and other agents. Each card invalidates a different simplifying assumption.

segments.label: Worked mechanism
segments.text: Computational backtracking does not imply physical reversal. A planner can return to another frontier record instantly, while a drone cannot teleport back through wind and obstacles. Execution cost and irreversibility must be represented if they matter to the real task. A warehouse robot may use A-star on a local occupancy grid while a scheduler coordinates peers and a controller handles motion. Layered systems are normal.

segments.label: Boundary and guarantee
segments.text: Partial observations and unknown dynamics break the fixed-state graph. Dynamic environments can invalidate edges while the plan is running. These settings motivate sensing, belief states, policies, online search, incremental replanning, and reinforcement or decision-theoretic methods. A learned heuristic can adapt guidance, but learning does not automatically provide admissibility or consistency. If guarantees matter, the learned estimate needs a bound, verification, or safe search wrapper.

segments.label: Transfer and takeaway
segments.text: Use the environment audit aloud: deterministic or stochastic, fully or partially observable, episodic or sequential, static or dynamic, discrete or continuous, known or learned, single-agent, cooperative, or competitive. The answers determine whether A-star belongs and what must surround it. Choose one prior application and classify it with every question in the audit. Any answer you cannot state is a modeling uncertainty, not permission to assume.

slides.title: Trace it, justify it, and decide when it belongs

segments.label: Concept framing
segments.text: The cumulative task has three parts. First, trace a weighted graph by showing every selected node, OPEN and CLOSED state, parent, g, h, and f update. Include a reopened state so duplicate policy becomes visible rather than hiding behind the word implementation. For the trace card, make one table row per expansion and record goal timing. A state generated early can still wait while a.

segments.label: Worked mechanism
segments.text: Second, justify heuristic claims. Use zero less than or equal to h less than or equal to h-star for admissibility, and h of n less than or equal to edge cost plus successor h for consistency. State edge-cost and termination assumptions beside the proof. For the proof card, separate heuristic admissibility from A-star optimality. The former is an inequality about h; the latter also depends.

segments.label: Boundary and guarantee
segments.text: Third, decide whether the model belongs. Choose among greedy best-first, A-star, uniform-cost, breadth-first, or a non-path-search method. Name the required guarantee, resource tradeoff, environment assumptions, and why the rejected alternatives fail the task. For the decision card, test whether the environment is a stable deterministic graph. If uncertainty, opponents, or continuous feedback dominate, say which richer model replaces or surrounds path search.

segments.label: Transfer and takeaway
segments.text: The durable sequence is trace, justify, decide. Arithmetic without a model is bookkeeping; a theorem without assumptions is a motivational poster; an algorithm name without either is horoscope reading for priority queues. Build the representation first, then earn the conclusion. Finish by marking one skill as secure and one as needing practice: exact trace, inequality proof, or environment-model diagnosis. Your next study step should target.
